itineraries.title: Tallinn in 2 Days: Old Town, Toompea, and Kadriorg
itineraries.subtitle: In 2 days, explore on foot and by tram, climbing from the Old Town to Toompea before heading to Kadriorg and the Seaplane Harbor.
itineraries.notes: Plan your trip for a Saturday and Sunday: many museums close on Mondays from October through April, and the Raeapteek pharmacy is closed on Sundays. The Town Hall interior can also be visited in the off-season by reservation. Its tower is open from June through September, and St. Olaf’s tower from April through October.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with average highs of 15 to 22 °C; July and August are also the rainiest months. From November through February, highs range from -1 to 4 °C, and daylight lasts only about 6 hours at the winter solstice. In freezing weather, wear shoes with good traction, as the climb up Toompea Hill follows sloping streets.

visits.text: Pass between the two round towers of Viru värav (Viru Gate) to enter the Old Town from the east. These are corner towers, rather than the gate itself. The gate dated to the 14th century. In 1888, the city demolished its buildings to make way for a horse-drawn tram but kept these two towers. Then head up Viru Street, a shopping street: Town Hall Square is a five-minute walk away.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.4 km in 6 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Carved dragon heads project from the Town Hall facade on Raekoja plats (Town Hall Square). These are gargoyles, waterspouts that channeled rainwater away from the walls. The Gothic building was rebuilt in 1402–1404. The city describes it as the oldest town hall in Northern Europe. On the spire, the weather vane depicts a city guard nicknamed Vana Toomas (“Old Thomas”); the current one is a copy from 1996. The tower is open to visitors from June through September. From September through May, the rooms can be visited by reservation, Monday through Friday; advance group bookings are also available on weekends.

The most surprising shop on the square is a pharmacy, Raeapteek. By 1422, it already had its third owner. It claims to be the oldest pharmacy in Europe still operating in the same building. Its 1695 price list offered marzipan, believed to soothe the heart and restore memory. Burned bees and stallion hooves were also sold here. The pharmacy is open Monday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. A small museum room displays old pharmacy tools.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.35 km in 5 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Slip into Katariina käik (St. Catherine’s Passage), a narrow alley linking Vene Street and Müürivahe Street. It runs alongside the wall of the former Dominican monastery; the preaching friars had been established here since at least 1246. Carved gravestones with worn Latin inscriptions are embedded in this wall. Across the alley, artisans’ workshops specialize in glass, ceramics, textiles, and jewelry. Come during daylight hours: the inscriptions are easier to read in good light.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.2 km in 3 minutes is correct.

activities.text: If you want to walk along the ramparts, climb Hellemanni torn (Hellemann Tower), at the end of Müürivahe Street. A wall walk—the guards’ passage along the top of the wall—starts here and runs for nearly 200 meters. It leads to Munkadetagune Tower and offers views of the city. The access stairs are steep, so keep your hands free. Admission starts at €4. From October 15 to April 15, the tower is open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

practical_info.tip: From October 15 to April 15, the tower is closed on Tuesdays. The rest of the year, it is open daily from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.

visits.text: Tallinn’s most striking painting is a dance of skeletons at Niguliste muuseum, housed in St. Nicholas’ Church. This Dance of Death, painted by Bernt Notke in the 15th century, shows Death leading people from every social rank: no one escapes. Only the beginning survives; the complete work measured 30 meters long. Then take the glass elevator up to the tower’s viewing platform. On Saturdays and Sundays at 4 p.m., a half-hour organ recital is held in the church. The museum is closed on Mondays from October through April.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are a short walk apart in Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.3 km in 5 minutes is correct.

visits.text: “Peek into the kitchen”: that is what Kiek in de Kök means in Low German, the language of merchants in the Hanseatic League, a medieval trading alliance. From this cannon tower built in 1475, guards could see right into neighboring kitchens. The full ticket, priced at €16, also includes the tunnels dug beneath the bastions, massive defensive structures added from the late 17th century onward. These tunnels served as shelters during the bombings from 1943 to 1945. Temperatures inside range from 7 to 10 °C, so keep a jacket with you.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.45 km in 8 minutes is correct.

visits.text: In 1684, a major fire destroyed all the wooden furnishings in Tallinna Toomkirik (St. Mary’s Cathedral). First mentioned in 1233, it is Tallinn’s oldest church. Coats of arms belonging to noble families, dating from the 17th to the 20th century, hang on the walls. These coats of arms served as epitaphs, plaques commemorating the dead. Swedish general Pontus De la Gardie and Russian navigator Krusenstern are buried here. The church is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Its 69 m bell tower can only be visited in good weather, outside services and concerts.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are just steps apart in Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.2 km in 3 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Toompea Castle, with its pink Baroque facade, houses the Riigikogu, Estonia’s Parliament. Right next door, construction of Pikk Hermann (“Tall Hermann”) began around 1360–1370. The national flag is raised there every morning at sunrise to the sound of the national anthem, then lowered at sunset. Replaced by the Soviet flag in 1940, it returned to its place on February 24, 1989. The interior can be visited by reservation, with free guided tours on weekdays for groups of at least ten people.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are just steps apart in Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.15 km in 2 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Russian right down to its onion domes, Alexander Nevsky Cathedral faces Estonia’s Parliament, and that is no coincidence. Built from 1894 to 1900, when Estonia belonged to the Russian Empire, it was intended to assert Russian dominance opposite Toompea Castle. Its towers house eleven bells, including the largest in Tallinn. Inside, look at the iconostasis, the partition covered with icons that stands in front of the altar. Photography is prohibited inside, and visitors are expected to wear clothing that covers their shoulders and knees.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are just steps apart in Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.35 km in 5 minutes is correct.

visits.text: The red roofs of the lower town spread out just below Kohtuotsa vaateplatvorm, a viewpoint on the northern side of Toompea Hill. Look for the spire of St. Olaf’s Church and the Town Hall tower rising above the rooftops. In the distance, the harbor, the Gulf of Finland, and the Pirita district line the horizon. The viewpoint is free and accessible day and night, year-round. It is often crowded; the light is most beautiful at sunrise and sunset.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.25 km in 4 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Continue another two hundred meters to Patkuli vaateplatvorm, Toompea’s other viewpoint. Here, the view looks down over the round towers of the city wall, with St. Olaf’s spire and the harbor beyond. To head back down, take the Patkuli Stairs, built in 1903: their 157 steps lead to Toompark, near Snelli Pond. In summer, cruise groups crowd the viewpoint: aim to arrive before 10 a.m. or after 5 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: Patkuli Stairs (157 steps), then on foot

visits.text: If you visit between April and October, climb the 232 steps of Oleviste kirik (St. Olaf’s Church) to the platform, 60 m above the ground. The church was first mentioned in 1267. It is named after Olaf II, the king of Norway who became a saint. Its spire now stands 123.7 m tall. From 1944 to 1991, the KGB, the Soviet political police, used it as a radio antenna and observation post. The tower is closed the rest of the year: admire the spire from Lai Street, then continue toward the harbor.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are just steps apart in Tallinn’s Old Town: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.25 km in 4 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Paks Margareeta (“Fat Margaret”) owes its nickname to its size: it is the largest tower in the city walls, measuring 25 m in diameter, with walls up to 5 m thick. Built from 1511 to 1530, it protected the harbor alongside Suur Rannavärav (Great Coastal Gate), the neighboring arch flanked by two towers. It served as a warehouse, then a prison, before becoming home to the Estonian Maritime Museum. Tip: a €30 combined ticket, valid for one week, covers this museum and Lennusadam, scheduled for the following day.

visits.text: In our opinion, the most beautiful facade on Pikk Street belongs to Mustpeade maja (House of the Blackheads). The Blackheads were a brotherhood of unmarried merchants and shipowners, often foreigners. Their patron saint, St. Maurice, was depicted as a Moor, a Black man: his head is carved above the entrance. The facade dates from 1597 and is in the Dutch Renaissance style. The painted door dates from the 1640s. The halls host concerts: check the program to end your evening with music.

to_next_leg.road_type: Tram 1 or 3 to the Kadriorg terminus

activities.text: Take tram 1 or 3 to the Kadriorg terminus: Kadrioru park (Kadriorg Park) begins there. Tsar Peter the Great established it in 1718. It covers about 70 hectares, roughly the size of a hundred soccer fields. Start by walking along Luigetiik, the Swan Pond, the park’s main body of water. The park also has a Japanese garden, whose first section was completed in 2011. It is open day and night: arrive around 10 a.m. so you can head to the palace as soon as it opens.

practical_info.tip: Tram 1 or 3, Kadriorg stop. The park is free and open 24 hours a day, every day of the year.

to_next_leg.justification: The two places are a short walk apart in Kadriorg Park: the routing engine returned a null value, and the current walk of 0.35 km in 5 minutes is appropriate.

visits.text: A tsar’s palace named after a woman: Kadriorg means “Catherine’s Valley.” Peter the Great had Kadrioru loss (Kadriorg Palace) built for his wife Catherine starting in 1718. Its great hall is one of the few well-preserved palace interiors from this period. Its ceiling depicts Diana and Actaeon, a scene from Metamorphoses, Ovid’s long Latin poem. The palace houses the Kadriorg Art Museum, devoted to European art from the 16th through the 20th centuries. Admission €15; closed Mondays from October through April.

to_next_leg.justification: The two places are a short walk apart in Kadriorg Park: the routing engine returned a null value, and the current walk of 0.6 km in 10 minutes is appropriate.

visits.text: Kumu, an Estonian art museum that opened in 2006, is built into the limestone slope of Lasnamäe Hill. Its Finnish architect, Pekka Vapaavuori, won the design competition back in 1994. Head to the third floor, devoted to art from 1945 to 1991, during the Soviet occupation. It displays socialist realism, the official art that glorified labor and the regime, alongside works by nonconformist artists who painted outside the rules. Admission €16, or €28 for three museums in Kadriorg. Closed Mondays; open until 8 p.m. on Thursdays.

to_next_leg.road_type: Taxi or rideshare (about 15 minutes); by tram, take line 1 to Põhja puiestee, then walk 1 km
to_next_leg.justification: Urban trip: the tram and walking (about 10 km/h) fall outside the train’s speed limits, and the fixed one-hour wait is unsuitable for a tram; I’m choosing a taxi, about 6 km in 15 minutes, with the tram still listed as an alternative.

visits.text: A bluish gloom fills the three concrete domes of Lennusadam (Seaplane Harbor), where a submarine rests at ground level. Tsar Nicholas II commissioned this hangar during World War I to house seaplanes, aircraft capable of landing on water. Its domes are very thin concrete shells, among the first of their kind. Step inside Lembit, an Estonian submarine ordered from the United Kingdom and launched in 1936. Outside, board the icebreaker Suur Tõll, moored at the dock. Admission €22; allow 2 hours.

to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre lennusadam et telliskivi loomelinnak, environ 1850 m de marche réelle comptés 2 km : l'ancienne durée de 5 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 23 min de marche.

activities.text: End the day at Telliskivi loomelinnak (Telliskivi Creative City). This creative district opened in 2007 on the site of a former Baltic Railway Company factory. Its ten buildings house more than 300 businesses, mostly in the creative industries. Stroll among the large murals, then step inside Fotografiska, a photography center that opened in 2019. Its cafe and restaurant are accessible without a ticket. On Saturdays, a flea market brings the site to life. Right next door, the street food stalls at Balti Jaama Turg market serve until 6 p.m. on Sundays.

practical_info.tip: Tram 1 or 2, Telliskivi or Balti jaam stops. The indoor Balti Jaama Turg market opens from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Saturday and from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Sundays.

seo.h1_title: Tallinn in 2 Days: Old Town, Toompea, and Kadriorg
seo.intro_paragraph: This 2-day weekend in Tallinn begins in the Old Town, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, then heads up Toompea Hill to its viewpoints. On the second day, the tram takes you to Kadriorg Palace and Kumu, followed by Seaplane Harbor and the creative district of Telliskivi. Everything is accessible on foot or by tram, with no car needed.

itineraries.title: Lahemaa in 3 Days: Manors, a Bog, and Seaside Villages
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Jägala Waterfall to Palmse and Sagadi Manors, then on to the villages of Altja and Käsmu.
itineraries.notes: From October through April, Palmse Manor is open Wednesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., except in January and February, when visits are limited to groups with advance reservations. Plan your visit around these opening arrangements. The three nights are spent in Palmse and then Käsmu, with a drive of about 1 hour 15 minutes to Tallinn on the last morning.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: June through August, with average highs of 19 to 22 °C in Tallinn and sea temperatures reaching about 18 °C in August. May and September are well suited to walking, with temperatures around 15 to 16 °C, but the manors close earlier starting in October. From December through February, highs hover around 0 °C and the days are very short: bring footwear suitable for snow.

activities.text: Pick up your rental car at Tallinn Airport, 5 km southeast of the city center, or in the city itself. This route does not linger in the capital. The E20 heads east toward Narva and Lahemaa National Park. Jägala Waterfall, your first stop, is about thirty minutes away.

practical_info.tip: From October through April, avoid starting on a Monday or Tuesday: Palmse Manor, which you will visit in the afternoon, is closed on those days.

visits.text: More than 50 m wide and about 8 m high, Jägala Waterfall (Jägala juga) is Estonia’s widest natural waterfall. Here, the river drops over a limestone cliff, the North Estonian Klint. The water gradually wears away this rock ledge: this erosion has caused the waterfall to retreat by as much as 17 cm per year. In winter, it freezes into a wall of ice, and a tunnel sometimes forms between the ice and the rock. The parking lot is just a few minutes away on foot.

activities.text: If you have an extra half hour, drive to the mouth of the Jägala River, 4.3 km downstream from the waterfall. A footbridge crosses the river where it flows into Ihasalu Bay, on the Gulf of Finland. Just before the sea, the Linnamäe hydroelectric power plant holds back the water behind an 11 m dam. Between the waterfall and the sea, the river is one of Estonia’s most prized fishing spots, rich in large trout and salmon.

practical_info.tip: Save this detour for a day when you have made a good start: Viru Bog, your next stop, takes more than two hours on its own.

to_next_leg.road_type: E20, then the road to Loksa

visits.text: The best way to understand Viru Bog (Viru raba) is to view it from above. Located 1.3 km from the parking lot, an 11.4 m wooden tower overlooks numerous pools nestled in the moss. This is a raised bog: accumulated peat has lifted it above the surrounding land. Its only water comes from rain, which is low in nutrients. Few plants tolerate these conditions; the sundew compensates by catching small insects. The upper platform holds a maximum of 25 people, and climbing the tower is prohibited during thunderstorms.

activities.text: The Viru Bog trail is 3.5 km long, almost entirely along a boardwalk, a path of wooden planks laid over the soft ground. A bog is a wetland where dead plants barely decompose because the water lacks oxygen. They accumulate and form peat, which grows about 1 mm thicker each year. Sphagnum, a moss that absorbs nearly 20 times its weight in water, is the main peat-forming plant. To return, follow the blue dots along the forest path: the full loop is 5.5 km.

practical_info.tip: From the E20, turn left at km 52 toward Võsu and Loksa; the parking lot is on the right. Stay on the boardwalk and do not smoke: despite all the water, a bog burns very easily.

to_next_leg.road_type: E20, then the road to Palmse

visits.text: Peaceful today, Palmse Manor was the birthplace of a conspirator. Peter Ludwig von der Pahlen, born here, became an officer and statesman in the service of Russia. In 1801, he was one of the organizers of the murder of Emperor Paul I. His family, German nobles who had settled in the Baltic states, owned the estate from 1676 to 1919. Admission costs €12 from May through September and €8 during the rest of the year, including an electronic guide. From October through April, the house is open Wednesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., except in January and February, when visits are limited to groups with advance reservations.

Exotic plants grow beneath the glass roof of Palmse’s orangery, much as they did in the winter gardens of historic manors. The surrounding park is free to enter. As you explore, you will come across the distillery, a barn, a bathhouse, and a swan pond. Three marked trails run through it: those of the lord, the lady, and the young lady of the manor. In the former ox barn, a free exhibition tells the story of the estate’s restoration, carried out from 1973 to 1986. Palmse was the country’s first fully restored manor complex.

activities.text: Palmse Manor offers a vodka tasting if you book at least 24 hours in advance. For €15 per person, you will taste five flavored vodkas while hearing about the history of alcohol production on the estate. A tasting of three Estonian wines is available for the same price.

practical_info.tip: Schedule the tasting for the end of the day: you will spend the night in Palmse, with no need to drive afterward.

visits.text: Originally Rococo, now Neoclassical: Sagadi Manor changed styles forty years after it was built. Rococo favors curves and delicate ornamentation; Neoclassicism prefers restrained lines inspired by classical antiquity. The von Fock family had the house built from 1749 to 1753, then remodeled it from 1793 to 1795. Inside, eight rooms retain their painted 19th-century ceilings. The manor is open daily, year-round, and a single €5 ticket also covers the Forest Museum.

You can operate a harvester, a machine that cuts down trees and removes their branches, on the simulator at the Sagadi Forest Museum. The “Journey into the Forest” exhibition, completed in 2022, occupies two floors. It tells the story of how people have used the forest throughout history. Life-size taxidermy animals, virtual reality headsets, and a meditation room inside a small sauna round out the visit. After the museum, walk around the park: some of its oaks are among the tallest in Estonia.

Lahemaa means roughly “land of bays”: four peninsulas divide its coastline between four bays. Established on July 1, 1971, it was the first national park in the Soviet Union, which Estonia was then part of. The Oandu Nature Center, 3 km from Sagadi toward Altja, introduces the park in a 150-year-old house that once served as a forestry administration office. Films and exhibitions explore the park’s natural environment and the uses of wood. From mid-September to mid-May, the center is open only on weekdays.

activities.text: Clear springs and marshy hollows: the 4.7 km Oandu Old-Growth Forest Trail passes through primary forest, meaning forest that has been very little altered by people. Each hollow holds a different wetland. Keep your eyes open: moose, wild boar, bear, and lynx tracks have been recorded here. Start with the “Path to the Primeval Forest” exhibition at the Oandu Nature Center, then set out from its parking lot, where the trail signs are visible near the road.

practical_info.tip: Allow about 1 hour 45 minutes for the walk and wear shoes that can handle mud.

visits.text: Altja, a fishing village first mentioned in 1465, has thatched log houses lining a single street. On the point, the fishing net sheds were reconstructed using old photographs and residents’ memories. Under Soviet occupation, the coast became a border zone: access to the sea was forbidden, and boats were destroyed or taken away. In 1971, the new national park selected Altja for restoration to its original appearance. The village tavern serves local dishes Friday through Sunday from 12 p.m. to 8 p.m., according to Visit Estonia.

activities.text: On the Oandu Beaver Trail, you are better off looking for signs than for the animal itself: beavers are so shy that they are almost never seen. The signs they leave, however, remain clearly visible. The 1 km trail follows a ridge above the rapids of the Altja River. Along the way, you can see dams, lodges made of branches, felled trees, and stumps gnawed to a point by beavers’ teeth.

practical_info.tip: The small five-space parking lot is on the right side of the road, about 4 km past Sagadi toward Altja.

activities.text: Next, follow the 3 km Altja Nature and History Trail loop, starting from the tavern parking lot. Eight small panels tell the village’s story along the route, which passes the village swing and crosses two bridges. From the tip of the cape, the view extends to the Vergi Peninsula. The trail also leads to Altja Suurkivi, a glacial erratic—a boulder transported and then left behind by ice—which stands 4.1 m high and measures 22.6 m in circumference.

practical_info.tip: Allow about 1 hour 15 minutes for a leisurely walk; the trail is maintained year-round.

visits.text: Since 1993, the Käsmu Maritime Museum has occupied a former border guard station. The building dates from 1894, when Estonia was part of the Russian Empire under the tsars. Founded by Aarne Vaik, this private museum brings together objects, photographs, and artworks relating to seafaring, fishing, smuggling, and the marine environment. It also manages Käsmu Lighthouse, built in 1891, which is open to visitors. Admission is €8 per adult and €18 for a family.

The light-colored facades of captains’ houses line the road: Käsmu still bears the nickname “village of captains.” From 1884 to 1931, a navigation school trained sailors here. Almost every family included a captain or a first mate, the captain’s deputy. The first ship built here, in 1697, was built for the baron of Palmse, whose manor you have visited. In the cemetery near the wooden chapel, the graves bear the names of many captains.

activities.text: Walk the 4.2 km Käsmu Nature and History Trail loop, starting at the chapel. It passes through Estonia’s highest concentration of glacial erratics. These boulders were deposited by the ice sheet, an immense layer of ice that covered Finland and Sweden, as it retreated about 10,000 years ago. The largest, Matsikivi, nicknamed the Hermit, stands about 4.7 m high and measures 14.7 m in circumference. The return route follows the village road.

practical_info.tip: Park near the chapel. During a ticketed event in the village, access to the trail requires a ticket.

activities.text: If the sunshine lasts into the evening, finish the day on Käsmu Beach, beside the bay. This bay was once one of the region’s major winter harbors: sailing ships sheltered here during the icy months. The water stays cool, as the sea reaches about 18 °C in August, at its warmest. The Viru Folk festival has been held in the village since 2008; its final edition is announced for August 2027.

practical_info.tip: Check the dates of the Viru Folk festival before booking: access to the village may require a ticket during the event.

activities.text: On the final morning, drive back to Tallinn: about 95 km via Võsu and then the E20, a journey of 1 hour 15 minutes. Then return the car at Tallinn Airport, 5 km southeast of the city center, or in the city, depending on your rental agreement.

practical_info.tip: Allow at least 30 extra minutes to return the car before a flight.

seo.h1_title: Lahemaa in 3 Days: Manors, a Bog, and Seaside Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary starts in Tallinn and heads to Lahemaa National Park, established in 1971 on Estonia’s northern coast. You travel from Jägala Waterfall to Viru Bog, then to Palmse Manor and Sagadi Manor. The final stretch follows the coast from the fishing village of Altja to the captains’ village of Käsmu.
seo.seo_hook: Lahemaa in 3 days: Jägala Waterfall, Viru Bog, Palmse Manor and Sagadi Manor, Altja’s fishermen, and Käsmu’s captains.
featured_list: Jägala: a natural waterfall more than 50 m wide
Viru: an 11.4 m tower above the bog pools
Palmse: a manor restored from 1973 to 1986, with free access to the park
Sagadi: the von Fock family manor and Sagadi Forest Museum
Altja: log houses and fishing net sheds
Käsmu: a maritime school from 1884 to 1931 and glacial erratics

places_taglines.EE::viru-raba: A boardwalk trail and an observation tower above a bog.
places_taglines.EE::palmse: A restored Baroque manor, an orangery, and a large park with free access.

highlights: Jägala Waterfall: over 50 m wide, the widest in Estonia
Viru Bog: 3.5 km along a boardwalk and an 11.4 m tower
Palmse: the von der Pahlen family’s manor, the country’s first fully restored estate
Sagadi: a Rococo manor remodeled in the Neoclassical style and the Sagadi Forest Museum
Altja: a fishing village documented as early as 1465, with reconstructed net sheds
Käsmu: a captains’ village and Estonia’s largest field of glacial erratics

itineraries.title: Pärnu, Soomaa, and Kihnu in 3 Days: Beach, Bogs, and Island
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, go from Pärnu’s beach to Soomaa’s bogs, then to the island of Kihnu and its traditions.
itineraries.notes: The crossing to Kihnu leaves from the port of Munalaid, about 40 km from Pärnu, and takes about 1 hour: book ahead, especially on holidays. Soomaa’s spring flood, known as the “fifth season,” generally arrives in late March or early April, well before swimming season in Pärnu.
itineraries.climate: For swimming, aim for July and August: in Pärnu, average highs reach 23 °C in July and 22 °C in August, and the sea is around 19 °C. In June, the air temperature reaches 20 °C, but the sea stays around 15 °C. Avoid winter for Kihnu: ice and low water levels can stop the ferry from running, as happened in February 2026.

visits.text: Red bricks facing stone walls gave the Red Tower (Punane torn) its name. It is Pärnu’s oldest surviving building. In the early 15th century, this corner tower in the city walls served both as a defensive structure and a prison. Beneath the roof, a small theater with a wraparound screen shows a 10-minute animated film covering 15,000 years of local history, starting with the last ice age. The theater seats only about ten people, so book your screening. The tower is closed on Mondays.

The only surviving 17th-century city gate in the Baltic states, Tallinn Gate (Tallinna värav) was spared when Pärnu demolished its fortifications in the 19th century. Before 1710, when the city was under Swedish rule, it bore the name of King Charles Gustav. Its current name comes from the road to Tallinn, which began here. Walk through the gate to reach Vallikäär, the former moat along the city walls, now a park with linden-lined paths, a fountain, and arched bridges.

Grand in scale and restrained in decoration, St. Elizabeth’s Church (Eliisabeti kirik) is built in the Baroque style. In 1741, Empress Elizabeth of Russia donated 8,000 rubles to build this Lutheran church, which bears her name and was consecrated in 1747. Its current organ dates from 1929. Of the old town’s three churches, this is the one most often open to visitors. In summer, it hosts concerts and an international organ festival: check the program when you arrive.

St. Catherine’s Church (Katariina kirik) is Orthodox, as its silhouette makes clear. Its large central dome is topped with a lantern, a small tower with windows. Four turrets surround it, and a bell tower with a pointed spire completes the ensemble. Empress Catherine II of Russia gave it to the city after a visit in 1764, hence its name. Construction was completed in 1768. The doors are not always open, so plan mainly to admire it from the street.

To understand Pärnu in a single visit, Pärnu Museum (Pärnu muuseum) is the best place to start. Its new permanent exhibition, which opened in February 2026, begins with the Pulli site on the banks of the Pärnu River, where people lived a little over 11,000 years ago. It is Estonia’s oldest known settlement. Another room explains how Pärnu initially developed as two towns, one on each bank: one founded by a bishop, the other by an order of German knights. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You will pass the Pärnu Mud Baths (Pärnu Mudaravila) on your way to the beach. These treatments, which involve applying mud to the body, were very popular during the Soviet era. This is also where the seaside resort began: as early as 1838, warm seawater baths were offered here in summer and a sauna in winter. That first building burned down during World War I. The current building, in the Neoclassical style—inspired by ancient temples—dates from 1927. It houses a spa: look at its facade from the fountain opposite.

If you enjoy Art Nouveau, the early 20th-century style featuring curved lines and plant motifs, take a detour to Villa Ammende. The merchant Hermann Leopold Ammende commissioned architects from St. Petersburg to design it for his daughter’s wedding. The house later served as a summer casino, a library, and then, during the Soviet era, a dental clinic. Restored in 1999, it now houses a restaurant and guest rooms. You can freely admire its facade from the street, and its garden hosts concerts.

activities.text: You will cross the old town along Rüütli, Pärnu’s pedestrian street, which takes five minutes to walk without stopping. At one end, Independence Square (Iseseisvuse väljak) commemorates a key date: on the evening of February 23, 1918, Estonia’s independence was publicly proclaimed here. At the other end, the children’s park has a carousel and, in summer, a fountain. For dinner afterward, most cafés and restaurants are in the old town and along Supeluse Street, which leads down toward the beach.

practical_info.tip: Pedestrian-only street: park outside the old town.

activities.text: In the evening, colored lights illuminate the fountains along Pärnu’s Beach Promenade (Rannapromenaad). This path follows the sand past playgrounds, miniature golf, ice cream shops, and restaurants, some of which play music until late. Renovated in 2021, the promenade is open year-round, day and night. Follow it to the end at sunset: it stops at the surfing area, where the coastal meadow trail you will walk on the last day begins.

practical_info.tip: Open year-round, day and night.

to_next_leg.road_type: Drive to the port of Munalaid (about 40 minutes), then take the ferry to Kihnu (about 1 hour)
to_next_leg.justification: Two segments: about 40 km by road from Pärnu to the port of Munalaid (40 minutes), then the ferry crossing to Kihnu (about 15 km, 1 hour); the stated duration excludes waiting time, which the itinerary adds.

visits.text: It’s best to start with Kihnu Museum (Kihnu muuseum): it explains why UNESCO protects the island’s culture. Since 2008, it has been on the intangible cultural heritage list, which recognizes living traditions. In the past, men would leave for weeks or months to hunt seals and fish. The women who remained on the island passed down songs, dances, wedding rituals, and crafts. The island’s isolation helped preserve these customs. Housed in a former school in Linaküla, the museum is open daily from May through August, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. (€5).

An onion-shaped dome crowns St. Nicholas Orthodox Church on Kihnu, in Linaküla, very close to the museum and cemetery. This stone building dates from 1784 and was originally used for Lutheran worship. It was transferred to the Orthodox community after the wave of conversions in the 1840s. Even today, most islanders are Orthodox. Before entering, notice the fence and colored-brick gateway, and be discreet if a service is taking place.

Locals call him Kihnu Jõnn: Captain Enn Uuetoa, born on the island in 1848, is buried near the entrance to Kihnu Cemetery. He commanded large ships without a compass or sextant, the instrument used to calculate one’s position from the sun. In 1913, he went down with his ship, the Rock City, off the coast of Denmark. His remains were brought back to the island in 1992. Visit quietly and never after sunset: this is the islanders’ rule, so as not to disturb the dead.

Made in England, dismantled, then reassembled piece by piece, Kihnu Lighthouse (Kihnu tuletorn) was erected in 1864 at the southern tip of the Pitkänä Peninsula. It is one of four cast-iron lighthouses still standing on the Estonian coast. Its light shines 29 m above the ground. From June 1 to August 27, it is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with admission costing €5; in May, it opens only on weekends. During the rest of the year, visits must be booked by phone.

In spring, the smell of tar drifts over Kihnu’s fishing harbor, in the northern part of Suaru Harbor. This is the season when fishermen repair their wooden boats and fish traps. The island’s traditional boats are moored here and are still in use. Motorcycles with sidecars, a distinctive feature of Kihnu, often wait on the dock while their owners are at sea. The harbor is freely accessible year-round: look without touching the fishing equipment.

activities.text: You’ll reach the island of Kihnu by ferry from the port of Munalaid, about 40 km from Pärnu by road. The crossing takes about an hour and arrives at the island’s harbor in the village of Lemsi. The ferry makes only a few round trips a day, and some departures sell out on holidays: book online with the ferry operator, Kihnu Veeteed. You can leave your car in the guarded parking lot at Munalaid or take a bus from Pärnu’s bus station.

practical_info.tip: Book your outbound and return trips at the same time, especially in summer and on holidays.

activities.text: If you choose just one way to explore Kihnu, take a bike and follow the Kihnu Reesuratas, whose name means “travel wheel”: a marked loop of about 23 km linking the island’s main sights. Kihnu measures just 7 km long by 3.3 km wide. At the harbor, bike rentals cost €5 for 3 hours or €10 for 24 hours, from May through September. Bring cash: the island has no ATMs, and cards are not accepted everywhere.

practical_info.tip: Bike rentals at the harbor from May 1 to September 30.

activities.text: Red for young girls, blue for older women, black for mourning: on Kihnu, the color of a skirt conveys a message. To see this craftsmanship up close, step into Njaputüe pued, a craft shop in Lemsi selling items made by island residents. The kört, the striped wool skirt worn by the island’s women, always has a red band at the bottom, whatever its color. The women do everything themselves, from shearing the sheep to dyeing the yarn.

practical_info.tip: Shop open from June 1 to August 31, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry crossing of about 1 hour to Munalaid, then drive via Pärnu to Soomaa
to_next_leg.justification: Two segments: the crossing from Kihnu to Munalaid (about 15 km, 1 hour), then about 85 km by road via Pärnu to Soomaa (1 hour 30 minutes); the 150 minutes cover travel time only, with waiting time added by the program.

visits.text: The Soomaa National Park visitor center in Kõrtsi-Tõramaa tells the park’s story through a boat: the haabjas, a dugout canoe carved from a single log, often aspen, whose sides are then spread apart. This craft has been on UNESCO’s list of traditions in need of urgent safeguarding since 2021. Only five master craftspeople capable of building one remain. The exhibition devoted to the dugout canoe opened in January 2026. In summer, the center opens daily: ask about trail and river conditions.

A meadow in summer, a lake in spring: that’s the view from the Tõramaa observation tower beside the Halliste River. It overlooks a wooded meadow, a grassland dotted with old oak trees. In late March or early April, snow melts faster than the park’s four rivers can carry it away, and water spills over the meadows and forests. This is Soomaa’s “fifth season.” Water levels can rise by a meter a day for three or four days. In summer, watch for birds from the top instead.

activities.text: You can stretch your legs on the Beaver Trail (Koprarada), which starts right next to the visitor center. About 1.8 km long, it crosses a spruce forest and then wet woodland before reaching Mardu Stream, where beavers live. Signs point out evidence of their work along the water. The first 660 meters of boardwalk are suitable for wheelchairs and strollers. During winter and spring floods, much of the boardwalk may be underwater: check at the visitor center.

practical_info.tip: The boardwalk is often flooded in winter and spring.

activities.text: If you visit between April and October, book a canoe trip with Soomaa.com: this local operator considers it the best way to get to know the park. The self-guided option covers about 12 km of river in 1 to 5 hours, including local transportation, for €30 per person with a minimum of two people. Before you set off, the team shows you how to handle the canoe, and beginners soon get the hang of it. During spring floods, guided trips even weave between trees in the flooded forest.

practical_info.tip: The usual season runs from April through October, as long as the rivers are not frozen; book ahead.

activities.text: You will walk above a bog on the Riisa Trail (Riisa rabarada), a 4.8 km boardwalk. A bog is a waterlogged area where dead moss accumulates without decomposing and forms peat. The trail passes pools and has eight stopping points and an observation tower. The first 1,220 meters are accessible to wheelchairs and strollers. The parking lot is on the road to Pärnu: save this trail for the following morning, before leaving the park.

practical_info.tip: To walk beyond the boardwalk, guides offer 3 hours of bogshoe hiking, from mid-June to mid-April.

visits.text: The Rannaniidu Trail makes a 600 m loop along a boardwalk above a marshy coastal meadow at the end of Pärnu Beach. An observation tower halfway along offers views of the bay. Cows come to graze here every spring, maintaining the meadow. Allow half an hour.

activities.text: The shallow water at Pärnu Beach (Pärnu rand) warms up quickly in the sun, making it popular with families. In 2010, it reached a record 33 °C. In summer, lifeguards watch over swimmers, and a Blue Flag, a certification of cleanliness and safety, is raised each day. The beach is a 15-minute walk from the center.

practical_info.tip: Lifeguards are on duty during the summer season only.

activities.text: According to a Pärnu legend, couples who kiss at the end of the breakwater (Pärnu muul) will love each other forever. This breakwater, about 1.5 km long, was built to make it easier for boats to enter the harbor. A walkway on pilings leads to a small beach near the lighthouse, then the rocks continue: wear closed-toe shoes.

practical_info.tip: Wear closed-toe shoes for the rocky section.

seo.h1_title: Pärnu, Soomaa, and Kihnu in 3 Days: Beach, Bogs, and Island
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary starts in Pärnu, a seaside resort in western Estonia, with its old town and sandy beach. You then take a ferry to the island of Kihnu, whose traditions are inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage List. Finally, you paddle through Soomaa National Park, known for its spring floods, before returning to the beach.
seo.seo_hook: Pärnu Beach, canoeing and bogs in Soomaa, and the island of Kihnu with its UNESCO-listed traditions: 3 days in western Estonia.

Kihnu: museum, Captain Kihnu Jõnn’s cemetery, and lighthouse dating from 1864

Pärnu Beach: swimming with lifeguards on duty, breakwater, and coastal meadow

itineraries.title: Saaremaa and Muhu in 4 Days: Kuressaare and Kaali Crater
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel across Muhu and then Saaremaa, from the Angla windmills to Kaali Crater and Sõrve Lighthouse.
itineraries.notes: Most sites are fully open from mid-May to early September, and several can only be visited by reservation during the off-season. Book the Virtsu-Kuivastu ferry at praamid.ee, especially on weekends, and allow about 2 hours to drive from Tallinn to Virtsu.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: June through August, with average highs of 17 to 19 °C and sea temperatures around 17 °C in July and August. May and September are also options (12 to 15 °C), but several sites reduce their hours. Avoid November through March: 7 to 9 hours of daylight per day, highs near 0 °C, and frequent rain or snow.
specialties: Moulins à vent et villages ruraux

activities.text: At the port of Virtsu, you will board the ferry to Kuivastu on the island of Muhu. The crossing takes about 30 minutes and covers just under 8 km of sea. In summer, ferries depart regularly from early morning until late evening. In winter, expect roughly one ferry per hour. Book your ticket in advance at praamid.ee: a camera will read your license plate and direct you to the priority lane.

practical_info.tip: Allow about 2 hours to drive between Tallinn and Virtsu. On summer weekends, the wait without a reservation can be long. If you miss a departure, the next ferry usually leaves 30 minutes later.

visits.text: Suggested first stop after the ferry: St. Catherine’s Church on Muhu, in the village of Liiva on the island’s main road. A chronicle mentions it as early as 1267. The present stone church dates from the late 13th century: a single nave beneath high whitewashed vaults, with no bell tower. In 1913, paintings of the Last Judgment were discovered beneath the plaster on the walls. Bombing in 1941 and the subsequent Soviet era damaged them: look for the surviving fragments on the walls.

A path through junipers leads to the edge of Üügu Cliff on Muhu’s north coast. The Estonian tourist board describes it as the island’s largest cliff. Do not expect a sheer drop: the rock face is about 5.5 m high. Cavities in the rock were carved by waves when the sea reached higher than it does today. The shoreline is now about 150 m away. The site is accessible year-round, at any time.

Koguva first appears in the records in 1532. That year, the master of the Livonian Order, an order of German knights that ruled the region, freed a village peasant named Hansken and all his descendants from serfdom. Serfdom required peasants to work for a lord. Muhu Museum occupies several buildings in Koguva: Tooma Farm, the birthplace of writer Juhan Smuul, the former school, and an exhibition of textiles from the island. Admission is €7. Open daily from May 15 to September 15, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: If you enjoy villages that have remained almost intact, set aside 30 minutes to walk around Koguva after visiting the museum. The farms and their dry stone walls, built without mortar, are protected as an architectural monument. Koguva is not an open-air museum: families live here, and most houses are privately owned. Follow the village map and the orange signs leading to the museum buildings.

practical_info.tip: Stay on the paths and do not enter yards, even when the gate is open. During the off-season, the museum is open Tuesday through Saturday.

activities.text: Ostriches on a Baltic island: the surprise is part of the visit. Muhu Ostrich Farm, in the village of Nautse, also raises emus, zebras, red kangaroos, alpacas, and Poitou donkeys. Children will find a playground, while parents can enjoy a picnic area and a shop. The farm opens daily from May 15 to September 15, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. in June, July, and August, and until 4 p.m. in May and September.

practical_info.tip: Outside this period, the farm does not receive visitors: save it for a summer trip.

to_next_leg.road_type: Väinatamm causeway between Muhu and Saaremaa

visits.text: Five wooden windmills on a hill: Angla has the only group of windmills on Saaremaa that retains its original appearance. In 1925, nine windmills stood on the hill, serving the village’s thirteen farms. Four of the remaining windmills are post mills: the entire body rotates around a large post to face the wind. The fifth, slightly taller windmill is a Dutch-style windmill built in 1927: a fixed tower with only the cap rotating. You can visit the interiors of the Dutch-style windmill and one post mill.

Small but rich in detail, Karja Church, about 2 km from the Angla windmills, is Saaremaa’s smallest medieval church. It dates from the early 14th century. Its stone sculptures depict St. Catherine holding a book and St. Nicholas beside a monk carrying a boat. The wall paintings combine grimacing devils with symbols whose meanings are debated, such as a pentagram, a five-pointed star. The church opens from June 15 to August 31, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Saturday.

activities.text: You can extend your stop at Angla Heritage Center, which opened in 2011 at the foot of the windmills. It brings together a museum of the island’s folk culture, old farm machinery, a café, and a shop. In summer, farm animals and poultry live on-site. Pottery, wool felting, and bread baking workshops are available by reservation. The site opens daily, until 8 p.m. from May through August and until 6 p.m. the rest of the year.

practical_info.tip: Book workshops a few days before your visit. In summer, a miller sometimes grinds flour in one of the windmills.

visits.text: 21.3 m: that is the maximum height of Panga Cliff (Panga pank), on Saaremaa’s north coast. The Estonian tourist board describes it as the highest rock outcrop in western Estonia and its islands. An outcrop is a place where the underlying rock is exposed at the surface. The cliff face extends for about 2.5 km. According to tradition, its highest point was once used for sacrifices offered to the sea. The site is open day and night, year-round.

activities.text: If you want to watch the sun set over the sea from Panga Cliff, visit Kaali before Panga and arrive here toward the end of the day. The site has picnic areas, a large wooden swing, and a sundial made of dolostone, a rock similar to limestone. The surrounding grounds are wheelchair accessible. Bring picnic supplies and a jacket for the evening.

practical_info.tip: In June, the sun sets very late: check the sunset time before planning your day.

visits.text: Kaali Crater is 110 m wide and 22 m deep, with a small lake at the bottom. A meteorite, a chunk of material from space, created it about 3,500 years ago. A study published in 2016 dates the impact to shortly after 1500 BCE. The meteorite broke into pieces at an altitude of between 5 and 10 km. The largest piece created this crater, and eight smaller craters surround it. The impact released roughly as much energy as the Hiroshima bomb. The site has stairs with handrails and is open year-round.

For the island’s ancient inhabitants, Lake Kaali was sacred. One tradition holds that it was where the sun went to rest. During the Iron Age, it was enclosed by a stone wall about 470 m long. The Kaali Meteorite and Limestone Museum, near the parking lot, tells the story of the impact and displays a 96 kg fragment of another meteorite, which fell in Sikhote-Alin, Russia. It is open daily from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. from May through September; during the rest of the year, visits are by reservation only.

This is Saaremaa’s must-see landmark: Kuressaare Episcopal Castle, one of Estonia’s best-preserved medieval fortresses. Construction began in the 1380s for the bishops of Saare-Lääne, who ruled the island and the west coast. Its limestone halls house the Saaremaa Museum. Expect steep stairs and low doorways. Admission is €12; open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. in June, July, and August, and Wednesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. during the rest of the year.

Large, pointed earth ramparts surround and protect the castle complex. These are bastions, low, angular fortifications designed to better withstand cannonballs. Their layout, modeled on the work of the Frenchman Vauban, was designed by engineer Erik Dahlbergh, who served Sweden. Beginning in 1861, the ramparts were gradually converted into a park. Walk around the park along the moat: the castle appears from a different angle at each bastion.

Plain on the outside, Kuressaare Town Hall houses Estonia’s largest painted ceiling in its second-floor hall. The building was constructed between 1654 and 1670 at the initiative of Count Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie, a Swedish statesman who governed the island. The ceiling was brought from Narva, a city in eastern Estonia, during a restoration. Across the street, the public weigh house (1663) was used to weigh goods. The tourist information office on the ground floor is open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

activities.text: If the sun is out, walk through the castle park to the Kuursaal, the spa resort’s recreation hall, which opened on June 11, 1889. Its terrace overlooks the castle. Kuressaare’s sandy beach begins just beyond the park and is well suited to families. Lifeguards are on duty from June 1 through August 31, from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.

practical_info.tip: In July and August, the sea temperature is around 17 °C.

activities.text: You can end the day at one of Kuressaare’s spas; the town has been a spa destination since the 19th century. Its first mud bath establishment opened in 1840, treating guests with mud found near the town. Several spas now offer day passes. It is a good way to unwind after visiting the castle, especially on a rainy day.

practical_info.tip: In summer, book your admission a day or two in advance.

visits.text: A 21 m concrete sword rises beside the road to Sõrve in Tehumardi. From your stop at the southern tip of the peninsula, plan a drive to this monument. It commemorates the nighttime battle of October 8, 1944. That evening, the advancing Red Army encountered retreating German troops in the darkness. The Soviet monument dates from 1966. A few hundred meters farther south, a granite stone placed in 2012 marks the approximate location of the fighting.

You will climb the 248 steps of Sõrve Lighthouse, a 52 m concrete tower built in 1960 at the southern tip of Saaremaa. An earlier lighthouse was already marking this cape in 1646. The previous stone lighthouse was destroyed in 1944. On a clear day, you can see as far as the Latvian coast. At the foot of the tower, the visitor center displays models of Estonian lighthouses and recounts the history of shipwrecks offshore. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. from late May through September 5, and by reservation during the rest of the year; adult admission is €7.

If military history interests you, set aside 1 hour for the Sõrve Military Museum, about a kilometer from the lighthouse. It occupies a barracks building dating from 1955, part of a former Soviet naval post. Its rooms cover both world wars on the peninsula, the Soviet era, and current NATO equipment. Some of the objects come from local residents and nearby battlefields. Your ticket also includes admission to the Sõrve Nature Museum in the same complex.

The Stebel Coastal Battery was a group of guns tasked with defending the coast. The Estonian tourist board describes it as Saaremaa’s most powerful and modern battery. It included two underground gun turrets, a command post, an observation tower, and a military camp. The observation tower has been preserved. To reach it, turn off the Sääre-Kaugatuma road at the 3 km mark. The command post is at the 4 km mark, about a hundred meters west of the road, near a concrete obelisk.

Small towers of flat stones stacked by visitors line Ohessaare Cliff on the west coast of the Sõrve Peninsula. This limestone cliff is about 500 m long and up to 4 m high. Its rock layers formed on the floor of an ancient sea. They contain numerous fossils. Pick up a flat stone on the beach and add it to a tower: it is the local custom. The site is accessible year-round.

activities.text: According to a Saaremaa legend, the giant Suur Tõll created the islets off Sõrve Point while chasing Vanapagan, the devil of Estonian folktales. From the lighthouse, walk to the end of the peninsula, facing the Irbe Strait toward Latvia. It is a good spot for birdwatching. Along the way, you will pass the ruins of the lighthouse’s rescue station, built in the early 20th century.

practical_info.tip: In summer, a restaurant and visitor center operate at the point. Bring a windbreaker, even in July.

seo.h1_title: Saaremaa and Muhu in 4 Days: Kuressaare and Kaali Crater
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary begins with the ferry from Virtsu and a night on the island of Muhu, around the village of Koguva. It then crosses Saaremaa via the Angla windmills, Panga Cliff, and Kaali Crater, continuing to Kuressaare Castle. On the last day, you head down the Sõrve Peninsula to its lighthouse.

Kuressaare: a medieval episcopal castle surrounded by bastions

itineraries.title: Tartu and Setomaa in 4 Days: Piusa, Suur Munamägi, Rõuge
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Tartu and its university to Seto villages, the Piusa caves, and Suur Munamägi.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Thursday: outside peak season, Tartu’s museums close on Mondays and often Tuesdays, while those in Setomaa close on Sundays and Mondays, and the Piusa center opens only on weekends. The Suur Munamägi tower opens every day, even in winter. Tartu is about 186 km from Tallinn.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with highs of 17 to 23 °C in Tartu; in spring, nightingales sing in the Rõuge valley. June and August are the rainiest months, so keep a rain jacket handy. Avoid November through March if you want to see everything: highs hover around 0 °C, lows around -7 °C, days are short, and several sites open only on weekends.

visits.text: Thirty-four bells ring out above Raekoja plats, Tartu’s Town Hall Square. This carillon plays every day at 9 a.m., noon, 3 p.m., 6 p.m., and 9 p.m. The current town hall, completed in 1789, is the third built on this site. In front of it, the Kissing Students fountain features a pair of students sculpted by Mati Karmin in 1998. The subject is no coincidence: life in Tartu revolves around its university. Arrive at the square shortly before noon to hear the carillon.

Leaning but still standing, Tartu’s Leaning House has stood on Town Hall Square since 1793. It tilts 5.8 degrees, more than the Leaning Tower of Pisa. The reason lies in its foundations. On the river side, it rests on the city’s old stone wall. On the other side, it stands on soft, marshy ground that is gradually giving way. The building now houses the Tartu Art Museum. It opens Wednesday through Sunday, staying open until 8 p.m. on Thursdays.

In 1632, King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden founded the University of Tartu. Its main building, with its columns, dates to 1809. The university’s Art Museum displays plaster casts of Greek statues, Egyptian mummies, and Immanuel Kant’s death mask, cast from his face. A narrow wooden staircase leads to the attic, where the student lockup is located. In the 19th century, unruly students were confined here and covered the walls and doors with carvings. The €18 combined ticket provides admission to all three university museums for one month.

Tartu’s most surprising facade belongs to the red-brick St. John’s Church (Jaani kirik). It is decorated with terracotta figures: saints, kings, children, fantastical animals, and devils. Each was modeled by hand in wet clay, so no two are alike. According to Tartu’s tourist office, no church in Europe retains as many from the Middle Ages. Burned during the fighting in 1944, the church was restored between 1989 and 2005. Its bell tower is open to visitors Tuesday through Saturday for €3.

Toomemägi, or Cathedral Hill, overlooks Tartu’s old town and the Emajõgi River. The Estonians had a wooden fortress here, destroyed by crusaders in 1224. In the 19th century, the hill was turned into a park. It has two bridges with opposing names. The Angel’s Bridge, dating to 1838, bears a Latin motto meaning “rest restores strength.” The concrete Devil’s Bridge was built in 1913. The park is free to enter: 30 minutes is enough to walk around it.

If you visit between May and September, climb the towers of Tartu Cathedral on Toomemägi. This brick Gothic church, begun in the 13th century, has been in ruins since the wars of the 16th century. In the 1760s, its towers were lowered from 66 m to 22 m to support cannons. A section rebuilt in the early 19th century for the university library now houses the University of Tartu Museum. Museum admission costs €12 in summer and €10 in winter, including the towers when they are open.

Look for the survey point marker on the floor in the entrance hall of the Tartu Old Observatory. From here, astronomer Friedrich Struve began the Struve Geodetic Arc: a chain of survey points stretching more than 2,820 km from the Arctic Ocean to the Black Sea. He wanted to determine Earth’s exact size and shape. UNESCO added the arc to its World Heritage List in 2005. Also see the Fraunhofer refracting telescope (1824), the largest of its time. In winter, check opening days before heading up.

The Estonian National Museum (Eesti Rahva Muuseum, ERM) stretches beneath a long, dark roof, 3 km from central Tartu. It occupies the former Raadi military airfield, long used as a Soviet bomber base. It is Estonia’s largest museum. The “Encounters” exhibition traces Estonian life from prehistory to the present. In the basement, “Echo of the Urals” introduces peoples whose languages are related to Estonian, such as the Setos, whom you will meet later. Allow 3 hours. The museum opens Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

activities.text: If you have 20 minutes left after the museum, walk around Lake Raadi in the park surrounding the ERM. This estate belonged to Raadi Manor, owned by the von Liphart family. This Baltic German family collected works of art. The National Museum moved here in 1922. The manor’s main building was destroyed during World War II. The park retains a rotunda and waterside picnic spots.

practical_info.tip: Parking at the ERM is free. Enter the museum through side A.

visits.text: To understand who the Setos are, start at the Värska Farm Museum (Seto Talumuuseum). The Setos are a small Orthodox ethnic group whose language, Seto, is closely related to Estonian. Three-quarters of their homeland, Setomaa, is now in Russia. The museum recreates the farm of a prosperous Seto family in the 1920s. Ten to fifteen people lived here, gathered around a large stove. The neighboring buildings house a smoke sauna, a forge, and a pottery workshop. Outside peak season, the museum opens Tuesday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Every May 6, on St. George’s Day, Värska’s Orthodox church celebrates its patron saint. The day ends in the afternoon with a village festival, the kirmaski. The church retains its early-20th-century iconostasis, the icon-covered screen separating the altar from the congregation. It also preserves a 17th-century icon of St. George painted on wood. Several leading figures in Seto culture are buried in the neighboring cemetery. Visits to the interior are by appointment: call the parish before coming.

An Art Nouveau villa, in the flowing style of around 1900, in the middle of a former military camp: this is General Reek’s House on the shore of Lake Õrsava. General Nikolai Reek spent his summers here, near the Estonian army training camp established in the 1920s. Because the original was too badly damaged, the house was rebuilt using the original plans and photographs. It serves as a visitor center. Its exhibition tells the story of the camp and Värska’s mud and mineral-water treatments. Outside peak season, it opens Tuesday through Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: Pressed fresh cheese, cold fermented-milk soup, thick porridge: the Seto Tsäimaja café serves Seto cuisine next to the Värska Farm Museum. Dishes arrive in handmade earthenware. The menu is written in Seto, giving you a chance to read a few words of the language. Try sõir, the Setos’ pressed fresh cheese. Milk, mushrooms, and fish play an important role in this cuisine, which is also shaped by Orthodox fasting traditions.

practical_info.tip: The café opens year-round, Monday through Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Group meals must be booked in advance.

activities.text: Walk around Lake Õrsava on a trail of about 5 km starting at the Värska school stadium. The path follows the shore and crosses several footbridges between the water and the pine forest. Part of it follows the old military camp road, where a few barracks are still standing. On the shore near the village of Õrsava, you will find a swimming area and a campfire pit. Save this walk for the end of the day, after the museum.

practical_info.tip: The official starting point is at the school stadium, but you can join the loop anywhere. Allow about 1 hour 15 minutes for the walk.

visits.text: Obinitsa Museum (Obinitsa Seto Muuseumitarõ) opened in 1995 in the village’s former library. Around 2,000 objects tell the story of Seto life, mainly between 1910 and 1940: tools, woven textiles, costumes, and photographs. One room explores the lives of Seto women a century ago. The small Orthodox chapel next door, called a tsässon, keeps the same hours as the museum. Ask about the “Rõivile!” workshop, where you are dressed in Seto costume while each piece is explained. In the off-season, the museum is open Tuesday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

The Setos call the best soloist in their traditional leelo singing a “Mother of Song.” In Obinitsa, the Mother of Song monument, erected in 1986, honors all these singers. In leelo, a soloist sings each line, then a choir repeats the end of the line and the entire line. UNESCO added it to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2009. Stones at the foot of the monument honor local singers. Walk up for views of the lake and the old village of Obinitsa.

Obinitsa’s cemetery draws more visitors than its church. People have been buried here for at least 1,500 years. The oldest graves, to the west, are marked with small stones. The Seto singer Hilana Taarka is buried here, as is Lidia Sillaots, who was behind the village museum’s creation. The current church dates from 1952, as the old one had been given to the school. Every August 19, the Feast of the Transfiguration, thousands of people come to honor their ancestors. The church interior can only be visited by reservation.

The temperature stays at 4 to 5 °C year-round in the Piusa Caves, former sand mines. From 1922 to 1966, sandstone (a rock made of sand) composed almost entirely of quartz was extracted here to make glass. Several thousand bats spend the winter here, from October to May, making this their largest refuge in the Baltic states. To keep visitors safe and avoid disturbing the bats, the galleries have been closed to visitors since 2006. A film and a 3D virtual tour at the visitor center show you inside. A guide then takes you to the viewing platform in the museum cave.

activities.text: Next, walk the Piusa Trail, a 1.4 km loop starting at the cave museum parking lot. It passes through the pine forest of the Piusa Caves Nature Reserve. Signs in Estonian and English introduce protected plants and animals. Just behind the museum cave lies the Piusa sand pit, which the tourist office calls “Estonia’s largest sandbox.” The trail is maintained year-round; allow 30 minutes.

practical_info.tip: From October to May, the visitor center is open only on Saturdays and Sundays, from noon to 4 p.m. In summer, it opens daily from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., but the bats have left the caves.

visits.text: At an elevation of 318 m, Suur Munamägi is the highest point in Estonia and the Baltic states. Its name means “Big Egg Hill,” referring to its rounded shape. At the summit, the 29 m observation tower dates from 1939. An elevator was added in 2005. On a clear day, you can see 50 km. The tower opens daily: from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. from April through August, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. in September and October, and from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. from November through March.

activities.text: If you have booked ahead, end the day at Mooska Farm in the village of Haanja. It keeps alive the smoke sauna tradition of Võromaa (the Võru region), which UNESCO added to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2014. This sauna has no chimney. A fire heats the stove’s stones for several hours, and its smoke fills the room. The guided tour lasts about 1 hour 30 minutes and takes you through three saunas. It introduces birch whisks, bundles of branches used during bathing, and ends with a tasting of sauna-smoked meat.

practical_info.tip: The farm welcomes visitors by reservation only. Allow at least 3 hours for a full sauna session.

visits.text: In spring, when the wild cherry trees bloom, nightingales fill Ööbikuorg, Rõuge’s Nightingale Valley, with song. This valley, 300 m long and 12 to 15 m deep, joins the Rõuge Valley and its seven lakes. To the north, it runs alongside an ancient hillfort whose earthen ramparts are still visible. At the edge of the valley, the Pesapuu observation tower has a platform 27 m above the ground, open day and night. The 450 m trail, with stairs and footbridges, is not cleared of snow in winter.

Climb the square bell tower of St. Mary’s Church in Rõuge. The current church dates from 1730. It replaces the one destroyed during the Great Northern War, fought between Sweden and Russia in the early 18th century. The altarpiece, depicting Christ on the cross, was painted in 1854. The organ was built in 1930 by the Kriisa brothers. In summer, the church stays open for visitors. Admission to the bell tower costs €1.50 per adult and €3 for a family.

This is the narrowest passage on the trip: Hinni Canyon, in the village of Nursi, 7 km from Rõuge. This gorge, carved into sandstone, is about 200 m long and 15 to 20 m deep. It is 6 to 10 m wide at the entrance but quickly narrows to 3 m. No other sandstone canyon this deep is known in Estonia. Footbridges, stairs, and handrails make it easy to walk through. Dogs are not allowed because the trail crosses private land.

activities.text: Rõuge Suurjärv is Estonia’s deepest lake, reaching 38 m. It is one of seven lakes lined up along the floor of the Rõuge Valley, linked by the small Rõuge River. According to a local legend, a church with silver bells sank into its waters during a war. The water’s color ranges from orange to light green, and its clarity varies greatly. Stop along the shore as you pass through town.

practical_info.tip: Allow 30 minutes to walk down to the lakeshore and back up. Nightingale Valley is a few minutes away by car, toward Haanja.

visits.text: From 1833 to 1877, physician Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald lived in Võru, in the house that now holds the Kreutzwald Memorial Museum. It was in Võru that he wrote Kalevipoeg, Estonia’s national epic: a long poem recounting a hero’s exploits. Built in 1793, his house is one of the oldest in town. The interior remains as it was when he lived there. The outbuilding displays works inspired by his writings and translations of Kalevipoeg. The museum is open Wednesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and until 6 p.m. from April through September.

activities.text: Extend your break along the 800 m Lake Tamula promenade, with its sandy beach. The town of Võru was founded beside this lake in 1784 at the request of Russian Empress Catherine II. A bronze statue of Kreutzwald, cast in Italy and unveiled in 1926, stands in a lakeside park. In summer, concerts bring the promenade to life, and lifeguards watch over the beach during the swimming season.

practical_info.tip: The beach and promenade are accessible year-round, day and night.

visits.text: Tartu residents call one of their neighborhoods Supilinn, or “Soup Town.” Its streets are named after vegetables and fruit: Herne (pea), Oa (bean), or Meloni (melon). This formerly poor neighborhood stretches along the right bank of the Emajõgi, just north of the city center. It consists mainly of two- or three-story wooden houses. Explore on foot toward the end of the day, when the low-angle light brings out the wooden facades.

activities.text: If the evening is mild, head down to the promenade along the Emajõgi, the “Mother River” that flows through Tartu. For 2024, when Tartu was a European Capital of Culture, the left bank was renovated between the Arch Bridge (Kaarsild) and the Peace Bridge. It now has tiered seating, terraces, and lounge chairs facing the water. The pedestrian-only Arch Bridge connects the city center to the Ülejõe neighborhood. Settle onto the tiered seating to watch the sun sink over the river.

practical_info.tip: The promenade is free to access. It begins at the Arch Bridge, near Town Hall Square.

seo.h1_title: Tartu and Setomaa in 4 Days: Piusa, Suur Munamägi, Rõuge
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary begins in Tartu, Estonia’s university city, and at the Estonian National Museum. It then heads south into Setomaa, home to the Setos, a small Orthodox ethnic group divided by the Russian border. Finally, you reach the Haanja hills, with Suur Munamägi and the lakes of Rõuge, before heading back north to Tartu via Võru.
seo.seo_hook: Tartu and southeastern Estonia in 4 days: the university, the Estonian National Museum, the Seto villages of Värska and Obinitsa, Piusa Caves, and Suur Munamägi.
